rationale: This is effectively a rank-weighted restatement of cash-based operating profitability (Ball et al. 2016) crossed with the Sloan accrual anomaly, and the stated logic is internally wrong — a product of two positively-signed ranks is monotone in each component, so it preserves both main effects rather than "isolating the joint cell."

Because |ib − oancf| is typically an order of magnitude smaller than total assets, the accrual term perturbs the denominator only trivially, leaving a signal that will be near-perfectly correlated with plain Novy-Marx gross profitability — a known anomaly with a cosmetic adjustment.

The regime-switch construction is a genuine conditional design rather than a repackaged known factor, but it deserves scrutiny because zeroing out all positive-accrual firms piles a large mass at exactly zero (mixing them with median cash-backed firms) and makes the short leg consist of low-profitability negative-accrual firms, an economically odd basket.

This is the Sloan accrual anomaly with the deflator swapped from assets to |operating profit| — the reasoning explicitly denies being a rescaled Sloan measure while computing exactly that — and the absolute-value denominator scrambles interpretation for loss and near-zero-profit firms even after winsorization.

Using the second moment of accruals (an accounting-discretion proxy à la Dechow–Dichev) as the conditioning variable is the most economically distinct idea in this batch, though the 5-period VOL of an annually updated accounting ratio risks being mechanically degenerate or driven by fiscal-year-update artifacts, so the sampling frequency must be verified before the result is believed.

The dynamic "profit improvement validated by cash conversion" framing is coherent and not a standard published anomaly, but the two legs are mechanically near-collinear (Δib/at − Δoancf/at overlaps directly with Δoiadp/at), so the composite may collapse to little more than the change in operating cash flow to assets and should be tested against that benchmark.
